=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

# Project Kestrel: Buyer-Side Review of the Seller Update and Disclosure Letter

**Basis and caveat:** I have only the Seller's summary of positions and the Disclosure Letter, not the full SPA mark-up or the underlying DD-002 to DD-012 documents. Points on clause mechanics should be checked against the actual draft. The legal statements below are general NSW and Commonwealth law points for the deal team and external counsel to confirm.

## 1. Threshold point: the "FINAL / agreed at principal level / market" framing

The cover material says these positions were "settled at principal level" and are "not intended to be re-opened", and that they reflect "standard" market terms. I would not accept either claim without checking.

- **Confirm internally** whether any principal-level agreement exists (term sheet, email, heads of agreement) and what it covers. If it exists, it likely covers headline price and perhaps cap and time limits, not carve-outs, disclosure mechanics, or the specific diligence findings. Those findings post-date any such agreement, and the Seller's own Disclosure Letter shows they are unresolved.
- The "market" ranges are the Seller's assertion. Even if a 10-20% cap and a roughly 1% basket are within range, market ranges apply to general warranties. They do not support applying the same limits to title, tax, fraud, or known-issue indemnities.
- The cover note is also inconsistent with the Disclosure Letter. It says Bluefen is "addressed", yet the Disclosure Letter (s2) concedes there is no consent. It calls the incident "not expected to be material", yet the Disclosure Letter (s6) says the investigation is preliminary and unquantified. Treat the summary as advocacy and the Disclosure Letter as the more reliable document, because it is a Seller admission of the facts.

## 2. Structural issue: the package neutralises our diligence findings

The Seller's terms work together:

1. **General disclosure** of the whole data room and public registers (Sch 7, DL 1.1-1.2).
2. **Buyer knowledge exclusion** covering anything the Buyer or its advisers knew or could have discovered (cl 8.3).
3. **Limitations applying to all Claims** unless expressly stated otherwise (cl 12.3/13, 9.3/12.8/20.5).
4. **Exclusive remedy and non-reliance** applying to all Claims of any nature.

Everything we have found in diligence is already in the data room, so none of it would be recoverable as a warranty claim. The known items alone total about **AUD 4.13m** (Riverlark 3.2m + bonuses 0.42m + Ironquay 0.18m + Sandbar 0.33m), before on-costs. That is about 17% of price and close to the whole AUD 4.8m cap. The cap would give little real protection because known problems are excluded and the rest is subject to a basket, de minimis, and time limit.

Known issues therefore have to be handled through **price, conditions, completion deliverables, and specific indemnities**, not warranties. That is the organising principle for our mark-up.

## 3. Issue-by-issue analysis

### A. Must-fix: deal-economics and certainty

**Riverlark (about AUD 3.2m; not repaid, no discharge)**
- The Seller proposes a release "following Completion". That is inconsistent with a debt-free/cash-free deal. We would own a company with live debt and security, and the change-control clause (8.1) could be triggered by the sale itself.
- **Ask:**
  - Payout letter from Riverlark before Completion.
  - Repayment at Completion out of the price, paid directly to Riverlark via the funds flow.
  - Release of all security delivered at Completion, including the PPSR financing change statement, ASIC charge release, and any share or guarantee security.
  - The Seller to bear break costs and fees.
- Confirm whether Riverlark holds security over the shares. If it does, it also affects the title position.

**Bluefen (about AUD 3.6m, about 30% of FY26 revenue; consent clause 11.2, conditions 11.3; no consent)**
- This is the biggest value risk. As an illustration only, 30% of a AUD 24m price is about AUD 7.2m of value tied to one customer.
- The Seller offers "reasonable endeavours" and would treat the consent as **satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent**. That is defective: a consent could be delivered with the 11.3 conditions unmet, or on adverse terms, and the condition would still be deemed satisfied.
- **Ask:**
  - Bluefen consent as a **condition precedent for the Buyer's benefit**.
  - The consent must be unconditional or on conditions acceptable to the Buyer, with the 11.3 conditions evidenced as satisfied and no adverse amendment to the contract.
  - Only the Buyer may waive it.
  - A long-stop date, with a Buyer termination right.
  - The Seller to bear the cost of any consent fee or concession.
  - Consider a price-adjustment or deferred-consideration fallback if the Buyer elects to waive.
- Also confirm whether Bluefen's data is in the DD-006 export (see below).

**Closing bonuses (DD-005, AUD 420,000; not in funds flow)**
- The Seller calls these "a matter for the Seller" but has not itemised them. They are triggered by Completion and will be paid by the company, so the Buyer would bear them economically.
- **Ask:**
  - Treat them as Seller transaction costs or debt-like items, deducted from the price or paid out of proceeds through the funds flow.
  - Include employer on-costs (superannuation, payroll tax, workers' compensation as applicable), which the Disclosure Letter says are unaddressed.
  - Add a specific indemnity for any additional Completion-triggered payments.
  - Request a full list of retention, change-of-control, and bonus arrangements, since others may exist.

**Fundamental / title warranties on the same cap and time limits**
- Reject this. Capacity and title go to whether we own what we are paying for. Standard position:
  - Cap at 100% of the price.
  - No basket or de minimis.
  - Extended claim period (6 years is the usual order, matching the contractual limitation period; confirm).
  - Unaffected by disclosure and knowledge.
- The only title evidence is the share register (DD-012), which the Seller itself says does not reflect any Buyer verification. Require ASIC extract and company records review, share transfer and certificates, confirmation of no options, convertible notes, pre-emption rights, shareholder agreements or encumbrances, and the Seller's authority and approvals.
- **Recourse risk:** Harbourglass Ventures may be a holding or fund entity that distributes proceeds. A cap is only as good as the covenant behind it. Consider an escrow or retention, a guarantee from a creditworthy parent, or W&I insurance (noting W&I excludes known issues, which is why specific indemnities remain necessary).

### B. Must-fix: legal risk and liability

**Ironquay IP (DD-004 cl 7.3; DD-010; AUD 180,000)**
- Ownership of SOW3 Project Materials transfers only on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 shows AUD 180,000 open, and there is no receipt or confirmatory assignment. If the materials are in the product, the company may not own part of its core IP.
- The existing indemnity is limited to the SOW3 payment, which misses the real exposure (ownership gap, infringement claims, remediation or re-development, licence fees, and disruption).
- **Ask:**
  - Payment by the Seller before Completion, with bank evidence.
  - A **completion deliverable**: Ironquay's confirmatory deed of assignment of all SOW3 IP, plus moral rights consents from individual authors.
  - A broadened indemnity covering losses from any defect in ownership of Ironquay-developed materials.
  - Review of other SOWs and contractor and employee IP assignments generally.
  - IP ownership warranties treated at fundamental level or with a higher cap.

**Data export incident (DD-006; about 1,240 records; investigation preliminary)**
- "Not expected to be material" is unsupported. The Disclosure Letter says the Seller does not know whether anyone accessed the file, the scope, or whether notification is required, and states no loss.
- Regulatory points to test with privacy counsel:
  - Whether the company is covered by the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) notifiable data breaches scheme. At about AUD 12m revenue, the small business exemption is unlikely to apply.
  - The 30-day assessment timeframe, which depends on when the incident was discovered. We do not have the dates, and it may already be running or have passed.
  - Contractual notification duties to customers, which may include Bluefen.
  - Potential regulator action and civil claims.
- **Ask:**
  - Incident timeline.
  - Forensic or investigation report and access logs.
  - Written confirmation from the unintended recipient of non-access or deletion, if obtained.
  - The company's notification assessment.
  - Whether the cyber insurer has been notified.
  - Which customers' data is affected.
- **Contract protection:**
  - A specific indemnity for all incident-related losses (investigation, notification, regulatory, customer claims, remediation), outside the cap, basket, de minimis, disclosure, and knowledge limits.
  - Consider a retention or escrow until the investigation closes.
  - Covenants for the Seller to conduct the response in consultation with the Buyer pre-Completion.
  - A bring-down of data protection warranties.

**Tax and IP "settled under the general regime"**
- Reject. Request a **pre-Completion tax indemnity** and a tax claims period tied to the relevant amendment periods (commonly 6-7 years in practice), outside the basket and the 18-month limit.
- No tax diligence materials were provided in what I reviewed. For a SaaS target, check R&D tax incentive claims, GST, payroll tax, and contractor and employee classification.
- Seek stronger IP warranties covering ownership, no infringement, open-source compliance, and assignment of contractor and employee work.

### C. Important: liability architecture

| Seller position | Concern | Buyer position |
|---|---|---|
| Cap 20% (AUD 4.8m) | Top of the Seller's own range; inadequate once known issues are excluded | Hold at 20% for general warranties only if all carve-outs below are accepted. Otherwise seek higher. |
| Basket AUD 250k (about 1.04% of price), **excess only** | A deductible basket removes the first AUD 250k permanently | **Tipping basket** (once exceeded, recover from the first dollar), and aggregation of related claims |
| De minimis AUD 25k | Relatively high; many SaaS claims are small and recurring | Lower, and aggregate related or same-cause claims |
| 18 months for general claims | Acceptable if it covers at least one full audit cycle; **not** acceptable for tax, title, or specific indemnities | Keep 18 months for general claims only; longer periods for the rest |
| Limits apply to "all Claims unless expressly stated" | The default is inverted | Limits apply **only to general Warranty Claims**; carve out fraud, wilful concealment, fundamental warranties, tax, and specific indemnities |
| Exclusive remedy and non-reliance on "all Claims of any nature" (9.3/12.8/20.5) | Could cut across specific indemnities, fraud, and statutory remedies | Carve out fraud and dishonesty, specific indemnities, and non-excludable statutory rights. Narrow the non-reliance clause. |

### D. Important: disclosure and knowledge

- **General disclosure (Sch 7; DL 1.1-1.2):** Resist it. Disclosure should be **specific**, against identified warranties, and fair enough to identify the nature and scope of the matter. Public registers and the "entire data room" should not qualify the warranties. Insist on an indexed, frozen copy of the data room (USB or archive) for evidence.
- **Staleness:** The Disclosure Letter speaks as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, and today is 6 November. Require an updated disclosure and a bring-down at signing. Disclosure after signing should not cure a breach, and if it reveals a material matter the Buyer should have a termination or walk-away right.
- **Buyer knowledge (cl 8.3):** Delete it. At minimum:
  - Limit it to the **actual** knowledge of named Buyer deal-team members.
  - Remove "advisers" and "discoverable" (constructive knowledge).
  - Add an express "no knowledge limit" clause (sandbagging). Australian law is not settled enough to rely on silence.
  - Specific indemnities should be unaffected by any knowledge or disclosure.
- DL 1.4 (no admission) is acceptable but should not limit the Seller's warranties or indemnities.

### E. Lower priority but needs follow-up

- **Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate; three at AUD 110,000):** The Seller calls them ordinary-course but the Disclosure Letter says it does not state whether they are unavoidable, terminable, accrued, or ordinary course. Three identical renewals of "related" suppliers suggest a possible split of a single commitment, so check them against internal approval thresholds and for related-party links.
  - **Ask:** signed or unsigned status, termination rights, payment timing, and prepayments.
  - Treat any committed or prepaid amounts as debt-like or in the working capital adjustment.
  - Add interim covenants preventing new commitments or renewals without Buyer consent between signing and Completion.
- **Office lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009):** The Seller's wording is carefully non-committal ("does not describe it as…", "does not state…"). Read the clauses ourselves for change-of-control or deemed-assignment wording. If there is any doubt, add a warranty and, where practical, a consent or notice as a Completion deliverable. These are probably manageable but should not rest on the Seller's characterisation.

## 4. Summary of recommendations

**Positioning**
1. Do not accept the "FINAL / market" framing. Confirm internally what was agreed at principal level, and reserve all positions in writing.
2. Mark up on the basis that the data room findings are handled by price, conditions, deliverables, and indemnities, not warranties.

**Conditions and Completion deliverables**
3. **Bluefen consent** as a Buyer-benefit CP, with satisfied conditions, no adverse change, a long-stop date, and a Buyer-only waiver.
4. **Riverlark:** payout letter, repayment at Completion from the price, and security releases delivered at Completion.
5. **Ironquay:** payment evidence and a confirmatory IP assignment, with moral rights consents.
6. **Title pack:** ASIC and register verification, share transfer documents, and confirmation of no encumbrances (including Riverlark share security).

**Price and funds flow**
7. Deduct the AUD 420,000 bonuses plus on-costs, and the Riverlark debt, in the funds flow. Review the Sandbar renewals and any similar debt-like items.
8. Consider a retention or escrow, or other credit support, for recourse against the Seller entity.

**Specific indemnities (outside cap, basket, de minimis, disclosure, and knowledge)**
9. Data incident (DD-006).
10. Ironquay and IP ownership (broadened beyond the SOW3 payment).
11. Pre-Completion tax.
12. Completion-triggered employee payments and on-costs.

**Liability terms**
13. Fundamental warranties (title and capacity): cap at price, no basket, extended period, unaffected by disclosure and knowledge.
14. Tax: longer claims period, outside the general regime.
15. Cap: 20% for general warranties only. Basket: tipping, not deductible. De minimis: lower, with aggregation.
16. Limitations apply only to general Warranty Claims. Carve out fraud and statutory rights from the exclusive-remedy and non-reliance clauses.

**Disclosure and knowledge**
17. Replace general disclosure with specific, fair disclosure. Exclude public registers.
18. Delete cl 8.3, or limit it to actual knowledge of named individuals, with an express sandbagging clause.
19. Require updated disclosure and a bring-down, no cure by post-signing disclosure, and interim operating covenants.

**Information requests to the Seller**
20. Incident timeline, forensic report, access logs, and notification assessment.
21. Full copies of DD-002 to DD-012 and a frozen data room copy.
22. Sandbar contracts and approval records.
23. Any other change-of-control, retention, or bonus arrangements.
24. Tax and R&D incentive records.
25. Lease and Mossvale clause text, for our own review.

If useful, I can next prepare a draft issues list for the Seller's counsel, or mark-up language for the carve-outs, specific indemnities, and the Bluefen and Riverlark CP and deliverable provisions.

  - Covenants for the Seller to conduct the response in consultation with the Buyer pre-Completion.
  - A bring-down of data protection warranties.

**Tax and IP "settled under the general regime"**
- Reject. Request a **pre-Completion tax indemnity** and a tax claims period tied to the relevant amendment periods (commonly 6-7 years in practice), outside the basket and the 18-month limit.
- No tax diligence materials were provided in what I reviewed. For a SaaS target, check R&D tax incentive claims, GST, payroll tax, and contractor and employee classification.
- Seek stronger IP warranties covering ownership, no infringement, open-source compliance, and assignment of contractor and employee work.

### C. Important: liability architecture

| Seller position | Concern | Buyer position |
|---|---|---|
| Cap 20% (AUD 4.8m) | Top of the Seller's own range; inadequate once known issues are excluded | Hold at 20% for general warranties only if all carve-outs below are accepted. Otherwise seek higher. |
| Basket AUD 250k (about 1.04% of price), **excess only** | A deductible basket removes the first AUD 250k permanently | **Tipping basket** (once exceeded, recover from the first dollar), and aggregation of related claims |
| De minimis AUD 25k | Relatively high; many SaaS claims are small and recurring | Lower, and aggregate related or same-cause claims |
| 18 months for general claims | Acceptable if it covers at least one full audit cycle; **not** acceptable for tax, title, or specific indemnities | Keep 18 months for general claims only; longer periods for the rest |
| Limits apply to "all Claims unless expressly stated" | The default is inverted | Limits apply **only to general Warranty Claims**; carve out fraud, wilful concealment, fundamental warranties, tax, and specific indemnities |
| Exclusive remedy and non-reliance on "all Claims of any nature" (9.3/12.8/20.5) | Could cut across specific indemnities, fraud, and statutory remedies | Carve out fraud and dishonesty, specific indemnities, and non-excludable statutory rights. Narrow the non-reliance clause. |

### D. Important: disclosure and knowledge

- **General disclosure (Sch 7; DL 1.1-1.2):** Resist it. Disclosure should be **specific**, against identified warranties, and fair enough to identify the nature and scope of the matter. Public registers and the "entire data room" should not qualify the warranties. Insist on an indexed, frozen copy of the data room (USB or archive) for evidence.
- **Staleness:** The Disclosure Letter speaks as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, and today is 6 November. Require an updated disclosure and a bring-down at signing. Disclosure after signing should not cure a breach, and if it reveals a material matter the Buyer should have a termination or walk-away right.
- **Buyer knowledge (cl 8.3):** Delete it. At minimum:
  - Limit it to the **actual** knowledge of named Buyer deal-team members.
  - Remove "advisers" and "discoverable" (constructive knowledge).
  - Add an express "no knowledge limit" clause (sandbagging). Australian law is not settled enough to rely on silence.
  - Specific indemnities should be unaffected by any knowledge or disclosure.
- DL 1.4 (no admission) is acceptable but should not limit the Seller's warranties or indemnities.

### E. Lower priority but needs follow-up

- **Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate; three at AUD 110,000):** The Seller calls them ordinary-course but the Disclosure Letter says it does not state whether they are unavoidable, terminable, accrued, or ordinary course. Three identical renewals of "related" suppliers suggest a possible split of a single commitment, so check them against internal approval thresholds and for related-party links.
  - **Ask:** signed or unsigned status, termination rights, payment timing, and prepayments.
  - Treat any committed or prepaid amounts as debt-like or in the working capital adjustment.
  - Add interim covenants preventing new commitments or renewals without Buyer consent between signing and Completion.
- **Office lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009):** The Seller's wording is carefully non-committal ("does not describe it as…", "does not state…"). Read the clauses ourselves for change-of-control or deemed-assignment wording. If there is any doubt, add a warranty and, where practical, a consent or notice as a Completion deliverable. These are probably manageable but should not rest on the Seller's characterisation.
